claims.text: Conventional cast FeNiCrMn HEA has relatively coarse grains.
The mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA have primarily been evaluated only in connection with corrosion resistance.
High-energy mechanical alloying of Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn elemental powders will produce a homogeneous nano/micro-scale composite.
Mechanical alloying followed by SPS is a viable powder-processing and consolidation route for high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical alloying followed by SPS will refine the grain structure of FeNiCrMn relative to conventional casting.
The refined SPS-processed FeNiCrMn microstructure will have higher yield strength than conventionally cast FeNiCrMn.
The refined SPS-processed FeNiCrMn microstructure will have greater ductility than conventionally cast FeNiCrMn.
Mechanical alloying can be conducted under an argon atmosphere before SPS.
SPS near 1400 °C under moderate pressure is an established processing condition for mechanically alloyed HEAs.
Controlling milling duration and SPS parameters will limit excessive grain growth in FeNiCrMn.
Controlled oxygen uptake during FeNiCrMn processing may form minor, finely dispersed oxide or interstitial complexes.
Grain refinement increases yield strength through the Hall–Petch effect.
A refined grain structure may improve FeNiCrMn ductility by making deformation more uniform.
Nanoscale precipitates formed during processing could provide additional precipitation strengthening.
The proposed nanoscale precipitates could strengthen FeNiCrMn without causing embrittlement.
SPS-processed FeNiCrMn will exhibit at least a 30% increase in yield strength relative to cast FeNiCrMn.
SPS-processed FeNiCrMn will exhibit a favorable strength–ductility trade-off relative to cast material.
Excessive oxygen or uncontrolled sintering parameters may produce brittle phases that counteract mechanical improvements.
Prior investigation of the mechanical behavior of FeNiCrMn produced by mechanical alloying and SPS is limited.
